svg.aria-label: Diagram: DNS peering and forwarding zones in Google Cloud; both are private zones that hold no records of their own, a forwarding zone taking its data from configured target name servers and a peering zone taking its data from the producer VPC network's own name resolution order; forwarding to private targets originates from the 35.199.192.0/19 source range, which spans 8,192 addresses and is reachable only from a VPC network or a connected on-premises network, so it needs an ingress allow rule for TCP and UDP port 53, a route to the target, and a return route for 35.199.192.0/19 whose next hop is in the same VPC network the request came from, with the target itself required to send the reply since a response from any other name server is ignored; forwarding cannot use transitive routing, demonstrated by the documented scenario where a VM behind a peered network can reach the on-premises name server directly yet forwarded resolution still fails, and the documented fix is a peering zone; DNS peering is one-way, follows the producer network's resolution order, and supports exactly one transitive hop for no more than three VPC networks; and DNS peering is a different service from VPC Network Peering, which does not automatically share DNS information and is not required for DNS peering to work
svg.title: DNS peering and forwarding zones: forwarding refuses to be transitive, peering is transitive exactly once
svg.text: Two private zones that hold no records. One refuses to be transitive; the other is, exactly once.
And neither has anything to do with VPC Network Peering from #81.
Both are private zones. Neither accepts a record.
FORWARDING ZONE — “the data comes from one or more configured target name servers.”
PEERING ZONE — “the data comes from the producer VPC network according to its VPC name
resolution order.” You borrow a whole resolution order, not a zone.
Both still obey #98: authorized networks, longest suffix, and NXDOMAIN rather than fallthrough.
Forwarding: four things must be true, and three are outside Cloud DNS
Queries to private targets come from 35.199.192.0/19 — 8,192 addresses, “used for all customers”,
reachable only from a VPC network or a connected on-premises network. Not from the internet.
1. FIREWALL — an ingress allow rule for TCP and UDP PORT 53. Both protocols, both directions’ kit.
2. ROUTE to the target — a subnet route, or a custom route. Not a TAGGED static route.
3. RETURN ROUTE for 35.199.192.0/19 — next hop in the SAME VPC network the query came from.
Not over the internet. Not via another VPC. This is the one people miss.
4. THE TARGET ITSELF must reply. A response from any other name server is IGNORED.
If nothing answers, Cloud DNS synthesises SERVFAIL. Cache: 60 seconds, or the TTL, whichever is less.
“Cloud DNS cannot use transitive routing to connect to a forwarding target.”
The documented invalid setup: on-premises joined to vpc-net-a; vpc-net-a peered to vpc-net-b with
custom routes exported and imported; the forwarding zone authorized for vpc-net-b.
TEST A — ask the metadata server for the forwarded name: FAILS, expectedly.
TEST B — ask the on-premises name server DIRECTLY for the same name: SUCCEEDS.
So the network is fine and the resolution is not. Connectivity is not the thing being tested.
THE FIX, from the same page: a PEERING zone in vpc-net-b targeting vpc-net-a, and the forwarding
zone authorized for vpc-net-a. Either order.
Peering: borrow another network’s resolution order, one way, one hop
CONSUMER network holds the peering zone. PRODUCER network does the looking up — and lookups
“follow the DNS producer network’s name resolution order”: its private zones, its forwarding
zones, its Compute Engine internal names, its alternative name server.
“DNS peering is a ONE-WAY relationship.” The producer gains nothing. Two directions = two zones.
“Transitive DNS peering is supported, but only through a SINGLE transitive hop … no more than
THREE VPC networks.” a → b → c works. A fourth does not.
Cross-organization peering is supported. It needs roles/dns.peer in the PRODUCER’s project.
The confusion worth killing outright
“DNS peering and VPC Network Peering are DIFFERENT SERVICES.”
• “VPC Network Peering doesn’t automatically share DNS information.” #81 moved subnet routes
and nothing else — names were never part of the deal.
• “Peering zones don’t depend on VPC Network Peering.” No VPC peering required, in either order.
The rule of thumb: if the answer lives on a name server, forward. If the answer lives in another
VPC network’s resolution order, peer. And when a forward must cross a network boundary to reach
its target, you need BOTH — peer to the network that can forward, and forward from there.
Forwarding reaches servers. Peering reaches resolvers. Only one of them crosses a VPC boundary.
